title: 論語 鄉黨第十
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 10, 〈鄉黨〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 10 of the Analects, 鄉黨 Xiāng dǎng, named, as every book is, from its first words ("In his home village…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book is unlike the others: it is hardly sayings at all, but a picture of the Master in his daily life, set down by people who watched him closely — how he spoke at home and at court, how he carried himself before his lord and as an envoy abroad, what he wore in each season, how he fasted, what he would and would not eat, how he sat, slept and rode in a chariot. Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: what the sage called the Way is never apart from everyday use, and so his disciples noted his every movement; and Yin Tun: reading it now, the sage seems to stand before your eyes — though he did not hold himself in by rule, his virtue was simply so full that every gesture met the rites of itself. Much of the detail is old court ritual, explained briefly in the notes from the commentaries. Two lines are among the best known in the book: when the stables burned, he asked whether anyone was hurt, and did not ask about the horses (10.12); and the closing lines on the hen pheasant on the hill bridge (10.18), which Zhu Xi thought must have lost some words. Zhu Xi prints the whole book as one chapter cut into sections; each section (10.1–10.18, as the edition marks them) begins a new card, and longer sections are cut where his commentary interrupts the text. Many modern editions divide the book more finely, into 27. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
孔子於鄉黨，
恂恂如也，
似不能言者。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Kong, in district and village,
earnest and plain he was,
seeming like one unable to speak.
sentences.i: Among the people of his home district, Master Kong was earnest and plain, as though speaking did not come easily to him.
sentences.n: The book is named 鄉黨 from its opening words. Zhu Xi prints it as a single chapter (舊說凡一章, 'the old account has it as one chapter'; He Yan's heading also says 凡一章) and divides it into sections; his heading says seventeen, but his copy marks eighteen, and we number those eighteen as passages (the finer numbering used in many modern editions runs to twenty-seven). Almost all of it describes the Master's bearing, dress, food and conduct rather than his sayings. Zhu Xi's heading quotes Yang Shi: the Way the sage speaks of never leaves daily use, so his disciples watched his every movement and recorded it in detail; and Yin Tun: how eager the disciples were to learn — there was nothing in the sage's looks, words or movements they did not carefully write down for later ages, so that reading it now he seems to stand before our eyes; yet the sage did not do these things stiffly — with virtue at its fullness, every movement fits the rites of itself, and a learner who wants to steep himself in the sage should seek him here. 孔子 'Master Kong', as outsiders name him: the book describes him from without. 鄉 and 黨 are units of local organisation (Zhu Xi on 6.3: 12,500 and 500 households); here, he says, they stand for the place where his elders and his clan live (父兄宗族之所在). 恂 xún (Zhu Xi: 相倫反): Zhu Xi glosses 恂恂 'the look of truthfulness and substance' (信實之貌); He Yan's Wang Su, 'gentle and respectful' (溫恭之貌). X如也 'X-like, he was' — a reduplicated descriptive word, 如 'in the manner of', and the assertion 也 — is the pattern of this whole book. 似…者 'like one who…'. Zhu Xi: he seemed unable to speak because he was humble and yielding and did not put himself ahead of others on account of his worth or knowledge.

sentences.t:
其在宗廟朝廷，
便便言，
唯謹爾。
sentences.l:
When he was at the ancestral temple or at court,
he spoke clearly and fully,
only carefully.
sentences.i: But in the ancestral temple and at court his speech was clear and full, and every word of it careful.
sentences.n: 朝 here is cháo 'court' (Zhu Xi: 直遙反, and so in the passages that follow), not zhāo 'morning'; 廷 tíng is the court's open hall. 便便 is read pián pián (Zhu Xi: 旁連反), not biàn 'convenient': Zhu Xi glosses it 辯也 'clear, discriminating in speech'. 唯…爾 'only…, that is all': 爾 here is not 'you' but a final particle, 'just so'. Zhu Xi: the ancestral temple is where the rites and laws are kept, the court is where government issues; there speech cannot be unclear, so he asked about everything in detail and said all that needed saying — only carefully, never loosely. He Yan's Zheng Xuan agrees: though fluent, he was careful and respectful (雖辦而謹敬, 辦 there for 辯). Zhu Xi sums up the section: it records how the Master's speech and looks differed in his home district, in the temple and at court.

sentences.t:
朝，與下大夫言，侃侃如也；
與上大夫言，誾誾如也。
sentences.l:
At court, speaking with the lower grandees, he was forthright;
speaking with the upper grandees, he was mild but unyielding.
sentences.i: At court, before the lord appeared, he talked frankly and directly with the lower grandees, and with the upper grandees agreeably but without giving way.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: this is at court before the lord has come out to hold audience (此君未視朝時也). He cites the Royal Regulations (王制): a feudal lord's upper grandees are his ministers (卿), and his lower grandees number five. He takes his glosses from Xu Shen's Shuowen (許氏說文): 侃侃 'firm and straight' (剛直), 誾誾 'agreeable, yet remonstrating' (和悅而諍). He Yan's Kong Anguo reads them otherwise: 侃侃 'easy and cheerful' (和樂之貌), 誾誾 'balanced and upright' (中正之貌). 侃 is kǎn in modern practice (Zhu Xi spells it 苦旦反, a departing tone); 誾 yín (魚巾反). 與 yǔ 'with'.

sentences.t:
君在，
踧踖如也，
與與如也。
sentences.l:
The lord present,
reverent and uneasy he was,
measured and composed he was.
sentences.i: Once the lord was there, he was respectful to the point of unease, yet his bearing kept its proper measure.
sentences.n: 君在 'the lord present': Zhu Xi and He Yan's Ma Rong both say this is when the lord holds audience (視朝). 踧踖 cù jí (Zhu Xi spells them 子六反, 子亦反): Zhu Xi, 'the look of one respectful and not at ease' (恭敬不寧之貌); Ma Rong, 'respectful'. 與與 yú yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲, or read as the ordinary word, yǔ): Zhu Xi and Ma Rong alike gloss it 'the look of deportment just as it should be' (威儀中適之貌); Zhu Xi adds Zhang Zai's view, that 與與 means never forgetting to face toward the lord, and says that reading also works. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records how the Master differed at court in serving those above and dealing with those below.

sentences.t:
君召使擯，
色勃如也，
足躩如也。
sentences.l:
When the lord called him to receive the guests,
his face changed,
his feet moved in measured turns.
sentences.i: When the lord called on him to receive visitors from another state, his expression altered and his step became measured and ceremonious.
sentences.n: 擯 bìn (Zhu Xi: 必刃反): Zhu Xi, the man the lord of the host state sends out to receive guests; He Yan's Zheng Xuan, when there were guests he was sent to meet them. 勃 bó: Zhu Xi, 'the look of a changed colour' (Kong Anguo: his colour always changed). 躩 jué (Zhu Xi: 驅若反): Zhu Xi and He Yan's Bao Xian gloss it 盤辟貌 / 槃辟貌, the look of turning and winding steps, the gait of ceremony. Zhu Xi: both come from respect for the lord's command.

sentences.t:
揖所與立，
左右手，
衣前後，襜如也。
sentences.l:
Bowing to those he stood with,
his hands went left and right,
his robe front and back hung trim.
sentences.i: As he bowed to the men standing with him in the line, moving his clasped hands now to the left, now to the right, the skirts of his robe front and back stayed neatly in place.
sentences.n: 所與立 'those with whom he stood': Zhu Xi, the others serving as receivers with him. He explains: the receivers number half the rank-count (命數) — for a high duke of nine ranks, five men — and they pass the message along in order; bowing to the man on his left he moved his hands to the left, to the man on his right, to the right. He Yan's Zheng Xuan says the same, adding that with each bow down and up (一俛一仰) the robe swung front and back. 左 and 右 are verbs here, 'to the left, to the right'. He Yan's text reads 左右其手 'turned his hands left and right', with 其. 襜 chān (Zhu Xi: 赤占反), 'the look of neatness' (整貌).

sentences.t:
趨進，
翼如也。
sentences.l:
Hastening forward,
winglike he was.
sentences.i: When he hurried forward, his clasped arms were held out like the wings of a bird.
sentences.n: 趨 is the quick, short-stepped walk of respect. Zhu Xi: he hastened forward with his arms spread in a clasp, upright and fine, like a bird spreading its wings (張拱端好如鳥舒翼). He Yan's Kong Anguo: 翼如 speaks of being upright and fine (端好).

sentences.t:
賓退，
必復命，曰：「
賓不顧矣。」
sentences.l:
The guest having withdrawn,
he always reported back on his charge, saying:
“The guest no longer looks back.”
sentences.i: Once the visitor had gone, he never failed to report to the lord: “The guest has left and is not looking back.”
sentences.n: 復命 'to return the command', to report that a charge has been carried out. He Yan's Kong Anguo: he reported to the lord that the guest had gone. 顧 gù 'to turn the head, look back': a guest no longer looking back has gone, and the ceremony of seeing him off is over. Zhu Xi: he reported it to release the lord from his respectful attendance (紓君敬也). Zhu Xi sums up: this section records the Master's bearing when he served his lord as receiver of guests.

sentences.t:
入公門，
鞠躬如也，
如不容。
sentences.l:
Entering the duke's gate,
bent low he was,
as if it could not hold him.
sentences.i: Going in through the gate of the duke's palace, he drew his body in and bowed low, as though there were not room for him to pass.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: 鞠躬 is bending the body; the duke's gate is high and wide, yet he went as if it could not take him in — respect at its height. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 'drawing in the body' (斂身). 容 here is 'to hold, to have room for', not 'bearing'.

sentences.t:
立不中門，
行不履閾。
sentences.l:
Standing, he did not stand in mid-gate;
walking, he did not tread on the threshold.
sentences.i: He would not stop in the middle of the gateway, and in passing through he never stepped on the sill.
sentences.n: 中門 'to be in the middle of the gate' (Zhu Xi: 中於門): between the side-posts (棖) and the central post (闑), where the lord goes in and out. 閾 yù (Zhu Xi: 于逼反) is the threshold (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo: 門限). Zhu Xi cites the rites: officers entering and leaving the lord's gate pass on the right of the central post and do not step on the threshold. He quotes Xie Liangzuo (謝氏): to stand in the middle of the gate would be to take the place of honour; to tread on the threshold would be careless (不恪).

sentences.t:
過位，
色勃如也，
足躩如也，
其言似不足者。
sentences.l:
Passing the lord's place,
his face changed,
his feet moved in measured turns,
his words seemed to fall short.
sentences.i: As he went past the place where the lord stands, though it stood empty, his expression changed and his step grew careful, and he spoke as though he had scarcely words enough.
sentences.n: 位 here is the lord's place, empty at this moment. Zhu Xi: it lies between the gate and the screen wall, where the lord stands (the spot called 宁); even though the lord is not there, one passing it must show respect and not slight it because it is empty; his words seemed not enough because he did not dare speak freely. He Yan's Bao Xian: passing the lord's empty place. 似…者 'like one who…', as in 10.1.

sentences.t:
攝齊升堂，
鞠躬如也，
屏氣似不息者。

morph.gloss: to bend, to stoop (in 鞠躬, Zhu Xi: 鞠躬曲身也)
one's own person, oneself (古者言之不出，恥躬之不逮)

sentences.l:
Holding up his hem, he went up to the hall,
bent low he was,
holding his breath as though not breathing.
sentences.i: Lifting the hem of his robe as he climbed the steps to the hall, he bent his body low and kept his breath in, as if he had stopped breathing.
sentences.n: 齊 is read zī here (Zhu Xi: 音咨), 'the lower hem of a garment' (Zhu Xi: 衣下縫; He Yan's Kong Anguo: 衣下曰齊); 攝 is 'to lift' (Zhu Xi and Kong: 摳). Zhu Xi: the rites say that, about to go up to the hall, one lifts the robe with both hands a foot off the ground, for fear of treading on it, stumbling, and losing one's composure. 屏 bǐng 'to hold in, store away' (Zhu Xi: 藏也); 息 is the breath going in and out of the nose; near the most honoured one, his breathing too was grave. Kong Anguo: all this is great care.

sentences.t:
出，降一等，
逞顔色，怡怡如也；
沒階，趨進，翼如也；
復其位，踧踖如也。

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
ill at ease, in awe (only in 踧踖, Zhu Xi: 踧子六反)
reverent, uneasy (only in 踧踖, Zhu Xi: 踖子亦反)

sentences.i: Coming out, once he was a step down he let his breath go and his face eased into contentment; at the foot of the steps he hurried forward with his arms spread like wings; and back in his own place he was once more respectful and watchful.
sentences.n: 等 děng is a step of the stair (Zhu Xi: 階之級). 逞 chěng 'to let loose' (Zhu Xi: 放也): as he drew away from the one he honoured, he let out his breath and relaxed his face; 怡怡 'glad and easy' (和悅). 顔 is the edition's form of 顏. 沒階 'to the end of the steps' (沒 mò 'to come to an end'; Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo: 盡). 趨 is to hasten to his place. Zhu Xi: in his place he was still 踧踖 — what remained of his respect. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 其位 as the place he had passed on the way in (来時所過位). Zhu Xi quotes Lu Deming (陸氏): the base text has no 進 after 趨, and the common copies that have it are wrong; Zhu Xi's own text prints it all the same, as do both our witnesses. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records the Master's bearing at court.

sentences.t:
執圭，
鞠躬如也，
如不勝。
上如揖，下如授；
勃如戰色，
足蹜蹜如有循。

morph.gloss: to bend, to stoop (in 鞠躬, Zhu Xi: 鞠躬曲身也)
one's own person, oneself (古者言之不出，恥躬之不逮)

sentences.i: When he carried the jade tablet as envoy, he bent low as though it were too heavy for him; he held it no higher than in a bow and no lower than in passing a thing to someone; a look of awe came into his face, and he walked with short, close steps, his feet hardly leaving the ground, as if following along something.
sentences.n: 圭 guī, Zhu Xi says, is the jade tablet a feudal lord receives as his charge (命圭); when he sends to visit a neighbouring state, a grandee carries it to establish good faith. He Yan's Bao Xian likewise: sent as the lord's envoy to a neighbouring state, he carried the lord's tablet. 勝 is read shēng 'to bear, to be equal to' (Zhu Xi: 平聲), not shèng 'to overcome'. Zhu Xi: carrying his lord's vessel, light as it is, as if he could not bear it — respect and care at their height; 上如揖，下如授 means he held the tablet level, his hands level with his heart, no higher than in a bow, no lower than in handing over. He Yan's Zheng Xuan explains the pair otherwise: 'high, as in a bow', because in handing over the jade one should be respectful; 'low, as in handing over', because one does not dare forget the rites. 戰色 'a face that trembles', Zhu Xi: fearful in look. 蹜 sù (Zhu Xi: 色六反): 蹜蹜 is lifting the feet in short, cramped steps; 如有循, Zhu Xi says, is what the Record calls 'raising the front of the foot and dragging the heel' (舉前曳踵) — walking without the feet leaving the ground, as if going along something. He Yan's text ends 如有循也, with 也.

sentences.t:
享禮，
有容色。
sentences.l:
At the rite of presentation,
he had an easy bearing and look.
sentences.i: At the presentation of gifts that followed, his face was open and pleasant.
sentences.n: 享 xiǎng 'to present' (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 獻也). Zhu Xi: after the visit of state (聘) comes the presentation, with a tablet and a jade disc (圭璧) and goods set out in the courtyard (庭實) — Zheng Xuan says the same, citing the Rite of Visits (聘禮). 有容色 'had bearing and countenance': Zhu Xi glosses it 'at ease' (和也), and quotes the Yili: 'let the breath out and fill the face' (𤼵氣滿容).

sentences.t:
私覿，
愉愉如也。
sentences.l:
At the private audience,
cheerful he was.
sentences.i: And when he met the host lord privately, with gifts of his own, he was openly glad.
sentences.n: 覿 dí 'to see, to have audience' (He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 見也). Zhu Xi: 私覿 is seeing the host lord with gifts of one's own (以私禮見); 愉愉 is more at ease still. Zheng Xuan: after the presentation he saw the lord with his private gifts; 愉愉 is a pleasant face. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records the rites the Master observed when visiting a neighbouring state for his lord. He then quotes Chao Yuezhi (晁氏): Confucius held office in Lu from the ninth year of Duke Ding until the thirteenth, when he went to Qi, and in that time there were no court visits or embassies at all; so perhaps the two items on receiving guests and carrying the tablet only record what Confucius said these rites should be.

sentences.t: 君子不以紺緅飾。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: The gentleman did not use dark red-blue or crimson for trimming.
sentences.i: The gentleman would not have his collars and cuffs edged in a dark red-shot blue or in crimson.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: 君子 here means Confucius. 紺 gàn (古暗反) is, he says, a deep blue with a glint of red (深青揚赤色), the colour of the clothes for fasting; 緅 zōu (側由反) is crimson (絳色), used in the three years' mourning to trim the 練 dress (練服) put on at a later stage of it; 飾 is the edging of the collar (領縁). He Yan's Kong Anguo: cloth dipped once (in the dye) is called 緅; 飾 is the edging of collar and sleeves; 紺 is the full colour of fasting clothes, and to trim with it would look like fasting dress; at the 練 stage of the three years' mourning clothes are trimmed with 緅, and to trim with it would look like mourning; so neither was used.

sentences.t: 紅紫不以為䙝服。
sentences.l: Red and purple he did not use for clothes worn at home.
sentences.i: He would not wear red or purple even in his clothes for home.
sentences.n: 䙝 is the edition's form of 褻 xiè 'intimate, for private wear'. 服 'clothing'. Zhu Xi: red and purple are mixed colours (閒色), not the proper ones, and are close to women's dress; 䙝服 is what one wears at home, and if he would not use them even for that, it follows that he would not use them for court or sacrifice. He Yan's Wang Su: home clothes are not for public occasions; when not even these are made in such colours, they have no place at all in formal dress.

sentences.t:
當暑，
袗絺綌，
必表而出之。
sentences.l:
In the hot season,
in unlined fine or coarse kudzu,
he always wore it on the outside, over something.
sentences.i: In hot weather, wearing a single layer of fine or coarse kudzu cloth, he always had something on underneath.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: 袗 zhěn is 'single, unlined' (單也); kudzu (葛) cloth that is fine is 絺 chī, coarse 綌 xì. 表而出之, he says, means putting on an under-robe first and then wearing the kudzu over it on the outside, so that the body should not show — as in the Odes' 'covering that crinkled kudzu' (蒙彼縐絺). He Yan's text reads 縝 for 袗 and 必表而出 without 之; his Kong Anguo reads it the other way about: in the heat he wore single clothes, and when he went out he put an upper garment on top (加上衣).

sentences.t:
緇衣，羔裘；
素衣，麑裘；
黃衣，狐裘。
sentences.i: His black robe went with lambskin, his white robe with fawnskin, his yellow robe with fox fur: each robe matched the fur beneath it.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: 緇 zī is black, and the lamb's fur is the skin of a black lamb; 麑 ní (研奚反) is a fawn, and white; the fox is yellow. The robe 衣 yī is worn over the fur (衣以裼裘) and is meant to match it. He Yan's Kong Anguo: the colours of the outer and inner garments match.

sentences.t:
䙝裘長，
短右袂。
sentences.l:
The home fur: long,
the right sleeve shortened.
sentences.i: For wear at home his fur was long, but he had the right sleeve made shorter.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: long because he wanted it warm; the right sleeve short to make work easier. He Yan's Kong Anguo says the same. 短 is a verb here, 'to make short'; 袂 mèi is the sleeve.

sentences.t:
必有寢衣，
長一身有半。
sentences.l:
He always had a sleeping garment,
long, a body and a half.
sentences.i: He always had a nightrobe, one and a half times his own length.
sentences.n: 長 is read cháng here by modern practice; Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 (zhàng, 'in length'). 有 yòu 'and' joins the numbers (as 2.4 十有五). Zhu Xi: when fasting, reverence comes first; one cannot sleep undressed, nor sleep in the bright robe (10.7), so there was a separate sleeping garment, and the extra half was probably (蓋) to cover the feet. He quotes Master Cheng: this slip is out of place (錯簡) and belongs after 齊必有明衣布 (10.7); Zhu Xi adds that then this item would join the bright robe and the changed food as one kind, and the at-home fur and the fox and raccoon-dog furs would stand together as another. He Yan's Kong Anguo: it is what is now called a 被, a coverlet.

sentences.t: 狐貉之厚以居。
sentences.l: The thick furs of fox and raccoon-dog were for home.
sentences.i: At home he wore the thick furs of fox and raccoon-dog.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: the fur of fox and raccoon-dog is deep, warm and thick; at home he chose it for comfort. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: he wore them at home for receiving guests. 狐貉之厚 'the thick ones among fox and raccoon-dog': 之 joins the furs to the quality picked out.

sentences.t:
去喪，
無所不佩。
sentences.l:
Mourning put off,
there was nothing he did not wear at his girdle.
sentences.i: Except when in mourning, he wore every pendant at his girdle.
sentences.n: 去 'to put off, set aside': Zhu Xi marks it 上聲 (qǔ); we give the modern qù, as elsewhere (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 去，除也). 喪 sāng 'mourning'. 佩 pèi 'to wear hung from the girdle'. Zhu Xi: the gentleman does not part with his jade without cause, and the bodkin (觽) and whetstone and the like are all worn too. Kong Anguo: when not in mourning, he wore all that should be worn.

sentences.t:
非帷裳，
必殺之。
sentences.l:
If not the curtain-skirt,
he always had it tapered.
sentences.i: Apart from the full-width skirt worn at court and at sacrifices, his skirts were always cut narrower at the waist.
sentences.n: 殺 is read shài here (Zhu Xi: 去聲), 'to reduce, to taper', not shā 'to kill'. 帷裳 'the curtain-skirt': Zhu Xi explains that the skirt of court and sacrificial dress is made of full widths of cloth like a curtain (帷), pleated at the waist and with no tapered seams at the sides; other garments, such as the 'deep robe' (深衣), whose waist is half the width of the hem, have no pleats but tapered seams. He Yan's Wang Su: garments always have tapered seams; only the curtain-skirt has none..

sentences.t:
羔裘𤣥冠，
不以弔。
sentences.l:
Lambskin and a black cap
he did not wear to condole.
sentences.i: He never went to offer condolences in lambskin and a black cap.
sentences.n: 𤣥 (U+24965) is the edition's form of 玄 xuán 'dark, black'. 弔 diào 'to condole with mourners'. Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo say the same: mourning takes white as its keynote, auspicious occasions black (喪主素，吉主𤣥); Zhu Xi adds that in condoling one must change dress, so as to grieve for the dead, and Kong that good and ill fortune have different dress.

sentences.t:
吉月，
必朝服而朝。
sentences.l:
On the first of the month,
he always put on court dress and went to court.
sentences.i: On the first day of each month he always went to court, dressed for it.
sentences.n: 吉月 is the first day of the month (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo: 月朔也), not 'a lucky month'. 朝 cháo both times: 'court dress' and 'to attend court'. Kong Anguo: the court dress is the deerskin-cap dress (皮弁服). Zhu Xi: the Master did this in Lu after he had retired from office. He sums up: this section records the rules of the Master's dress; and he quotes Su (蘇氏): these are miscellaneous records of the lesser rites left in the writings of the Kong family, and not only about Confucius.

sentences.t:
齊，
必有明衣布。
sentences.l:
When fasting,
he always had a bright robe, of cloth.
sentences.i: For the fast before a sacrifice he always kept a clean robe of plain cloth.
sentences.n: 齊 is read zhāi here and in the next unit (Zhu Xi: 側皆反), 'to fast, to purify oneself before a sacrifice' (= 齋; He Yan's text writes 齋). Zhu Xi: when fasting one must wash and bathe, and on finishing the bath put on the bright robe, which keeps the body bright and clean; it is made of cloth. He adds that after this a slip — the sleeping garment of the previous section (10.6) — has dropped out (此下脫前章寢衣一簡). He Yan's Kong Anguo: a cloth robe for after washing and bathing. He Yan's text reads 齋必有明衣布也, with a final 也.

sentences.t:
齊必變食，
居必遷坐。
sentences.l:
Fasting, he always changed his food;
where he stayed, he always moved his seat.
sentences.i: While fasting he always changed what he ate, and moved from where he usually sat.
sentences.n: 食 is shí 'food' here; Zhu Xi gives it no reading note. Zhu Xi: changing the food means not drinking wine and not eating strong-smelling plants (不茹葷); moving the seat means changing one's usual place. He Yan's Kong Anguo: changing the usual food, and changing the usual place. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records how carefully the Master kept the fast; and he quotes Yang Shi: fasting is how one comes into contact with the spirits, so one makes oneself clean to the utmost and changes what is usual, to be wholly reverent.

sentences.t:
食不厭精，
膾不厭細。
sentences.l:
Rice — he did not refuse it finely polished;
minced meat — he did not refuse it finely cut.
sentences.i: Rice hulled clean and white he was glad to have, and raw meat sliced thin — though he did not insist on them.
sentences.n: Book 10 now turns to the Master's food and drink, and this section (10.8) runs over ten units. 食 here is read sì, 'cooked grain, rice' (Zhu Xi: 食音嗣…食，飯也; as 疏食 in 7.15), not shí 'to eat'. 精 'fine' is rice well hulled (Zhu Xi: 精，鑿也). 膾 kuài is raw meat cut fine — Zhu Xi: the raw flesh of ox, sheep or fish, sliced and then cut, is called 膾. 不厭 is literally 'did not reject': Zhu Xi says it means he counted these good, not that he insisted on having them so; rice fine nourishes a man, meat coarse can harm him. He Yan has no comment here.

sentences.t:
食饐而餲，
魚餒而肉敗，
不食。
色惡，
不食。
臭惡，
不食。
失飪，
不食。
不時，
不食。
sentences.l:
Rice gone sour and off in taste,
fish gone soft and meat spoiled —
he did not eat.
Colour bad —
he did not eat.
Smell bad —
he did not eat.
Cooking amiss —
he did not eat.
Not in season —
he did not eat.
sentences.i: Rice that had soured or turned, fish that had gone soft, meat that had begun to rot — none of these would he eat. Nor would he eat what had lost its colour or smelled wrong, what was underdone or overdone, or what was out of its season.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi's readings: the first 食 is sì 'rice' (食饐之食音嗣); 饐 yì (於冀反), 餲 ài (烏邁反), 飪 rèn (而甚反; modern rèn). Zhu Xi: 饐 is rice spoiled by heat and damp, 餲 its taste turned; fish going bad is called 餒, meat putrefying 敗. 色惡 and 臭惡 are food not yet spoiled whose colour or smell has changed — 臭 is 'smell' in general (read xiù), and 惡 è 'bad' says which. 飪 is the measure of rawness and doneness in cooking. 不時 is, for example, grain not grown to fullness or fruit not yet ripe. All of these can harm a man, so he did not eat them; 不食 'he did not eat' is shí each time. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 饐 and 餲 are changes of smell and taste; fish spoiled is 餒; 失飪 is missing the point between raw and cooked. His Zheng Xuan reads 不時 differently: 'not at the times' — not at morning, evening or midday, the hours of meals.

sentences.t:
割不正，
不食。
不得其醬，
不食。
sentences.l:
Cut not square —
he did not eat.
Not getting its sauce —
he did not eat.
sentences.i: Meat not cut square he left alone, and he would not eat a dish without the sauce that belonged to it.
sentences.n: 割 'to cut' is the carving of meat; 正 here is 'square, true'. 其醬 'its sauce': Zhu Xi says each meat has the sauce proper to it. Zhu Xi: meat not squarely cut he would not eat, not leaving what is correct even in haste; he adds that in the Han, Lu Xu's mother (陸續之母) never cut meat other than square and cut her onions to the inch — a fine nature that happened to match this. Without its sauce he would not eat, disliking a dish incomplete; neither of these harms a man, but he would not eat carelessly for the sake of taste. He Yan's Ma Rong gives an example: minced fish without mustard sauce he did not eat.

sentences.t:
肉雖多，
不使勝食氣。
唯酒無量，
不及亂。
sentences.l:
Meat, though plentiful —
he did not let it outweigh the rice.
Only wine had no measure —
not reaching disorder.
sentences.i: However much meat there was, he never let it outweigh the rice. Wine alone he did not measure out, but he never let it bring him to disorder.
sentences.n: 食 is again sì 'rice' (Zhu Xi: 食音嗣), and 量 is liàng 'a measure' (量去聲). 勝 Zhu Xi leaves unmarked; we read shèng 'to overcome, outweigh', the word of his own paraphrase (不使肉勝食氣), not shēng 'to bear' as in 如不勝 (10.5). 氣 is literally 'breath, vital force': the meat must not overpower what the grain gives. 唯 wéi 'only'. Zhu Xi: in eating, grain is the main thing, so meat is not let outweigh it; wine is for joining men in gladness, so he set no quantity, only taking drunkenness as the limit and stopping short of disorder. He quotes Master Cheng: 'not reaching disorder' means not only that the mind is not thrown into disorder — even the blood and breath must not be disordered; to be warmed through, and no more, is right. He Yan has no comment on this unit.

sentences.t:
沽酒市脯，
不食。
sentences.l:
Bought wine, market dried-meat —
he did not take.
sentences.i: Wine bought from a shop and dried meat from the market he would not touch.
sentences.n: 沽 and 市 are both 'to buy' here (Zhu Xi: 沽、市皆買也) — 沽 is 'to sell' in 9.12, but the word served for both sides of a trade. 脯 fǔ is dried meat. 不食 covers the wine too: 'he did not take (them)'. Zhu Xi: he feared they might not be fine and clean and might harm him — the same thought as not tasting Kangzi's medicine (10.11). He Yan has no comment.

sentences.t: 不撤薑食。
sentences.l: He did not take away the ginger at meals.
sentences.i: Ginger he never had cleared from the table.
sentences.n: 撤 chè 'to clear away'; 薑 jiāng 'ginger'; 食 shí 'food, the meal'. Zhu Xi: ginger clears the mind (通神明) and drives off foulness, so he did not have it removed. He Yan's Kong Anguo ties it to the fast: 撤 is 去 'to remove'; during a fast strong-smelling things (薰物) were forbidden, but ginger, though pungent, does not smell, so it was not removed.

sentences.t: 不多食。
sentences.l: He did not eat much.
sentences.i: And he never ate more than he needed.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: he ate enough and stopped, with no greed in his heart. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 不過飽 'never beyond full'. Both commentaries comment on this apart from the ginger clause before it, and both glosses read as eating in general, not ginger alone.

sentences.t:
祭於公，
不宿肉。
祭肉不出三日。
出三日，
不食之矣。
sentences.l:
Sacrificing at the duke's,
he did not keep the meat overnight.
Sacrificial meat did not go past three days.
Past three days,
it is not eaten.
sentences.i: Meat he brought back from the duke's sacrifice he did not keep even one night. His own sacrificial meat he did not keep beyond three days; after three days it would not be eaten.
sentences.n: 祭於公 is assisting at the sacrifice of the lord of the state. 宿 sù is 'to keep overnight'. Zhu Xi: the meat of the offering (胙肉) received at the duke's sacrifice was given out as soon as he came home, without waiting a night — not holding back the spirits' bounty. The meat of his family's own sacrifice he gave away within three days, for after three days it would spoil and people would not eat it, which would be to slight the leavings of the spirits; still, it could wait a little longer than the lord's gift. He Yan's Zhou Shenglie: the portions of the victims received from assisting at the lord's sacrifice were distributed on his return, not keeping back the spirits' bounty; and his Zheng Xuan: the second clause is about his own family's sacrifice; past three days it is not eaten, which would slight the spirits' leavings.

sentences.t:
食不語，
寢不言。
sentences.l:
At meals, no conversing;
in bed, no talking.
sentences.i: Over his food he held no conversation, and once he had lain down he said nothing.
sentences.n: 食 shí 'eating'; 寢 'to lie down to sleep'. Zhu Xi distinguishes the two words for speaking: answering or telling others is 語 (read yǔ here), speaking of one's own accord is 言. He quotes Fan Zuyu: the sage's mind does not wander — at the time to eat he eats, at the time to sleep he sleeps, and talk then is out of its time. And Yang Shi: the lungs govern the breath and the voice comes from them; in sleeping and eating the breath is blocked, and talking might harm it — a reading Zhu Xi says also works (亦通). He Yan has no comment.

sentences.t:
雖疏食菜羹，
瓜祭，
必齊如也。
sentences.l:
Even coarse rice, vegetable broth,
melon — he made the offering,
always gravely.
sentences.i: Even when the meal was only coarse rice, vegetable broth and a melon, he set aside the offering from each, and always with a solemn face.
sentences.n: 疏食 shū sì 'coarse rice' (Zhu Xi: 食音嗣; as 7.15); 菜羹 cài gēng is broth of vegetables. Zhu Xi explains the offering: the ancients, at every kind of food and drink, set out a little of each in the space between the dishes as an offering to the first men who made food and drink — not forgetting the root. Confucius made the offering even from poor things, and made it with reverence — the sage's sincerity. 齊如 'grave-looking' (Zhu Xi: 嚴敬貌; He Yan's Kong Anguo the same): Zhu Xi marks no reading, and we read zhāi, the word of the purifying fast of 10.7, whose gravity it describes. Variant: Zhu Xi quotes Lu Deming (陸氏) that the Lu Analects has 必 for 瓜, and the first collation witness (Ruan's 1816 text) reads so: 雖疏食菜羹，必祭，必齊如也 'even with coarse rice and vegetable broth, he always offered, always gravely' — no melon. He Yan's Kong Anguo, reading 瓜, speaks of 'three things' (rice, broth, melon): though meagre, they were offered with reverence. Zhu Xi sums up 10.8: it records the measure Confucius kept in eating and drinking. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: the sage ate like this not to satisfy mouth and belly but to nourish breath and body without harming life; yet what the sage would not eat, those who indulge the palate sometimes eat, desire getting the upper hand so that they have no time to choose.

sentences.t:
席不正，
不坐。
sentences.l:
The mat not square —
he did not sit.
sentences.i: Until his mat lay straight he would not take his seat.
sentences.n: 席 xí is the mat one sat on; 正 'set straight, square'. A section of a single line. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: the sage's mind rests in what is correct, so he would not stay in a place that was not correct, small as the matter was. He Yan has no comment.

sentences.t:
鄉人飲酒，
杖者出，
斯出矣。
sentences.l:
At the villagers' wine-drinking,
when those with staffs went out,
then he went out.
sentences.i: When the people of his district met to drink together, he left as soon as the old men with their staffs had left, and not before.
sentences.n: 鄉人飲酒 is the district's ceremonial drinking: He Yan's Kong Anguo says its rite centres on the old, and when the old had finished and left, Confucius followed them out. 杖者 'those with staffs' are the old: Zhu Xi says men of sixty carry a staff in the district (六十杖於鄉). 斯 here is 'then, thereupon'. Zhu Xi: before they had gone he did not dare go first; once they had gone he did not dare stay behind.

sentences.t:
鄉人儺，
朝服而立於阼階。
sentences.l:
When the villagers held the exorcism,
in court robes he stood on the eastern steps.
sentences.i: When the villagers went round driving out the demons of sickness, he put on his court dress and stood on the eastern steps.
sentences.n: 儺 nuó (Zhu Xi: 乃多反) is the rite of driving out pestilence; Zhu Xi says the Rites of Zhou put it in the charge of the Fangxiang shi (方相氏). 朝服 cháo fú 'court robes' (朝 read cháo as in 10.1). 阼階 zuò jiē are the eastern steps (Zhu Xi: 東階也). Zhu Xi: though 儺 was an ancient rite, it came close to play; that he still attended it in court dress shows there was nothing into which he did not put sincerity and reverence. Some say (或曰) he feared it would startle the spirits of his forebears and of the five household sacrifices, and wished them to rely on him and be at peace. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records Confucius's conduct in his district. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 儺 drives out the demons of pestilence; fearing it would startle his forebears, he stood in court dress on the eastern steps. Variant: He Yan's text reads 立阼階, without 於 'on'.

sentences.t:
問人於他邦，
再拜而送之。
sentences.l:
Sending to ask after someone in another state,
he bowed twice and saw him off.
sentences.i: When he sent a messenger with greetings to someone in another state, he bowed to him twice as he saw him off.
sentences.n: 問 here is 'to send to inquire after, to send greetings to'. 之 is the messenger. Zhu Xi: he bowed to the messenger as he left, with the reverence he would have shown on seeing the friend himself; He Yan's Kong Anguo says the same. Variant: He Yan's text reads 再拜送之, without 而.

sentences.t:
康子饋藥，
拜而受之。曰：「
丘未達，
不敢甞。」

morph.gloss: Kangzi — Ji Kangzi, a grandee of Lu

sentences.i: When Ji Kangzi sent him a gift of medicine, he bowed as he took it, and said: “I do not know enough about this, and will not venture to try it.”
sentences.n: 康子 is Ji Kangzi 季康子, the Lu grandee of 2.20 and 6.6 (the commentaries do not name him here; Yang Shi below calls the giver a grandee, 大夫). 饋 kuì 'to send as a gift'. 丘 is Confucius's personal name, used of himself. 達 'to understand thoroughly' — what the medicine was and what it did. 甞 is the edition's form of 嘗 cháng 'to taste'. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: whenever food is given, one tastes it and then bows; medicine not understood he dared not taste; to accept it and not drink it would empty the gift, so he told the giver this — and so drinking what may be drunk and not drinking what may not are both contained here. And Yang Shi: when a grandee sends a gift, to bow and accept it is the rite; not tasting what one does not understand is care about illness; telling him so is straightforwardness. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records Confucius's sincerity in dealing with others. He Yan's Bao Xian: Kangzi gave Confucius medicine; Kong Anguo: not knowing its nature, he did not taste it, and this was the rite. Variant: He Yan's text reads 不敢甞之, 'dare not taste it'.

sentences.t:
廏焚。
子退朝，曰：「
傷人乎？」
不問馬。
sentences.l:
The stables burned.
The Master, coming back from court, said:
“Any people hurt?”
The horses — he did not ask.
sentences.i: There was a fire in the stables. Home from court, the Master asked: “Is anyone injured?” About the horses he asked nothing.
sentences.n: 廏 jiù is the edition's form of 廄 'stable'; 焚 fén 'to burn'. 退朝 'to withdraw from court' — 朝 read cháo. 傷人乎 'hurt — anyone?'. Zhu Xi: it was not that he did not care for horses, but his fear that men had been hurt was so great that he had no leisure to ask; to value men and hold beasts cheap is as it should be. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: valuing men and slighting beasts; 退朝 is coming home from the Lord of Lu's court. Neither commentary says whose stables they were.

sentences.t:
君賜食，
必正席先甞之。
君賜腥，
必熟而薦之。
君賜生，
必畜之。
sentences.l:
When the lord bestowed food,
he always set his mat straight and first tasted it.
When the lord bestowed raw meat,
he always cooked it and offered it.
When the lord bestowed a live beast,
he always reared it.
sentences.i: Cooked food sent by his lord he would taste first, sitting on a mat set straight. Raw meat from his lord he had cooked and presented at his ancestral altar. A live animal from his lord he kept and raised.
sentences.n: Three gifts, three responses: 食 shí cooked food, 腥 xīng raw meat (Zhu Xi: 生肉), 生 a living animal. 薦 jiàn 'to present (to the forebears)'; 畜 xù 'to rear'. Zhu Xi: cooked food might be leavings (餕餘), so he did not offer it to his forebears; straightening his mat and tasting first was as though he faced the lord; 'first tasted' implies he then gave the rest away. Raw meat he cooked and offered to his forebears, honouring the lord's gift. Rearing the live animal was humaneness toward the lord's kindness: without cause he would not dare kill it. He Yan's Kong Anguo: it was reverence for the lord's kindness; after tasting he gave it away; 薦 is offering to his forebears. Variant: He Yan's text reads 先甞, without 之.

sentences.t:
侍食於君，
君祭，
先飯。
sentences.l:
Attending the lord at a meal,
when the lord made the offering,
he ate first.
sentences.i: When he sat at a meal with his lord, he began eating while the lord made the offering.
sentences.n: 侍食 'to attend at a meal' with a superior. 祭 is the small offering before eating (10.8). 飯 fàn 'to eat' (Zhu Xi: 扶晚反). Zhu Xi cites the Rites of Zhou: when the king ate his full meal, the steward (膳夫) handed him the offering and tasted the food, and only then did the king eat. So one attending at the lord's meal does not make an offering himself while the lord makes his, but eats first, as though tasting the food for the lord — not daring to take the part of a guest. He Yan's Zheng Xuan says the same: when the lord made the offering he ate first, as if tasting it beforehand (the archived text of his comment writes 先飲 'drank first').

sentences.t:
疾，君視之，
東首，
加朝服，
拖紳。
sentences.l:
Ill, and the lord came to see him:
he turned his head to the east,
laid his court robes over him,
and drew the sash across.
sentences.i: Once when he was ill and his lord came to visit, he had his head turned to the east, his court dress laid over his body and its great sash on top.
sentences.n: 首 is read shòu, the verb 'to turn the head toward' (Zhu Xi: 首去聲), as against shǒu 'head'. 拖 'to draw, trail': Zhu Xi marks 徒我反, which would give a modern duò; modern practice reads tuō, which we give. 紳 shēn is the great sash of formal dress (Bao Xian: 紳太帶). 朝服 cháo fú 'court robes'. Zhu Xi: the head to the east was to receive the breath of life (生氣); lying ill he could not dress and tie his sash, yet could not meet his lord in everyday clothes, so he had the court robes laid on his body and the sash drawn over them. He Yan's Bao Xian: the Master was ill, lying under the south window with his head to the east; he had his court robes laid on him and the sash drawn across, not daring to see his lord except in court dress.

sentences.t:
君命召，
不俟駕行矣。
sentences.l:
When the lord's command summoned him,
not waiting for the yoking, he set off.
sentences.i: When his lord sent for him, he did not wait for his carriage to be made ready but set out on foot.
sentences.n: 召 zhào 'to summon'; 俟 sì 'to wait for'; 駕 'to yoke (the horses to the carriage)'; 行 xíng 'to go'. 矣 marks the thing done. Zhu Xi: he hurried at the lord's command, setting out on foot, and the carriage, once yoked, followed him; He Yan's Zheng Xuan says the same. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records the rites by which Confucius served his lord.

sentences.t:
入太廟，
每事問。

morph.gloss: the Grand Temple — of the Duke of Zhou, in Lu

sentences.l:
He entered the Grand Temple;
about each thing he asked.
sentences.i: When he went into the Grand Temple, he asked about every detail.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi notes only 重出 'a repeat': these are the opening words of 3.15 (子入大廟，每事問), and the English is the one given there, with 'he' for 'the Master', since this text has no 子. The edition writes 太廟 here, 大廟 there; both are read tài miào, the temple of the Duke of Zhou in Lu. 每事問 puts the object first: 'each thing (he) asked about'. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: he had gone in to assist his lord at a sacrifice; the Grand Temple is the Duke of Zhou's temple.

sentences.t:
朋友死，
無所歸，曰：「
於我殯。」
sentences.l:
A friend died,
with no one to go home to; he said:
“Lay him out at mine.”
sentences.i: When a friend died with no family to take him in, he said: “Let him lie in his coffin at my house.”
sentences.n: 無所歸 'nowhere to return to': He Yan's Kong Anguo explains, no near kin. 殯 bìn is to coffin the dead and keep the body until burial. Zhu Xi: friends are joined by what is right; when one died with nowhere to go, he could not but lay him out. Kong Anguo: it shows how he valued the kindness of friends.

sentences.t:
朋友之饋，
雖車馬，
非祭肉，
不拜。
sentences.l:
A friend's gifts,
even carriage and horses —
if not sacrificial meat,
he did not bow.
sentences.i: For gifts from a friend he did not bow, even for a carriage and horses — only for meat from a sacrifice.
sentences.n: 車馬 'carriage and horses', the weightiest of gifts; 車 chē. Zhu Xi: friends share their goods as a matter of right (通財之義), so even for so weighty a gift he did not bow; for sacrificial meat he bowed, honouring the friend's forebears as he would his own kin. He Yan's Kong Anguo also explains the not bowing by the right of sharing goods. Zhu Xi sums up: this section records what Confucius held right between friends.

sentences.t:
寢不尸，
居不容。
sentences.l:
Asleep, not like a corpse;
at home, no formal bearing.
sentences.i: He did not sleep sprawled out like a dead man, nor did he sit about at home as if on ceremony.
sentences.n: 尸 shī 'corpse' is a verb here, 'to lie like a corpse'. Zhu Xi: 尸 is lying flat on the back like a dead man; 居 is being at home; 容 is formal bearing. He quotes Fan Zuyu: not lying like a corpse was not that he disliked resembling the dead; slack and idle breath never settled in his body, and though he stretched out his limbs he was never sprawling. Without formal bearing at home was not slackness either — only that he was not as when offering sacrifice or receiving guests: the ease of 申申夭夭 (7.4). He Yan's Bao Xian: lying on the back with the four limbs spread out like a dead man; Kong Anguo: the reverence of household life is hard to keep up for long (so he did not keep formal bearing). Variant: the first collation witness (Ruan's 1816 text) reads 居不客, which would make it 'at home he did not behave like a guest'.

sentences.t:
見齊衰者，
雖狎，
必變。
見冕者與瞽者，
雖䙝，
必以貌。
sentences.l:
Seeing one in mourning dress,
even an intimate,
his look always changed.
Seeing one in the ceremonial cap, or one blind,
even if seen informally,
always with due bearing.
sentences.i: If he saw someone in mourning, even a close friend, his expression changed. Someone in a ceremonial cap, or a blind man, he always treated with formal courtesy, however often they met.
sentences.n: For the rest Zhu Xi refers back to the earlier book (餘見前篇), that is, to 9.9. 齊衰 zī cuī is mourning dress; 冕 the ceremonial cap of men of rank; 瞽 gǔ 'blind'. 見 jiàn 'to see'; 與 yǔ 'and'. 狎 xiá is long familiarity; 䙝 (the edition's form of 褻, xiè) is meeting at leisure; 貌 is the bearing the rites require. Zhu Xi: 狎 means already close and familiar; 褻 means seeing someone informally (燕見); 貌 is ritual courtesy. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 狎 is long familiarity; Zhou Shenglie: 䙝 is seeing often; even so he must keep his bearing, which is the rite. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子見齊衰者, with 子 'the Master' as subject.

sentences.t:
凶服者式之。
式負版者。
sentences.l:
One in mourning dress — he bowed to him at the crossbar.
He bowed at the crossbar to one carrying the registers.
sentences.i: From his carriage he bowed to anyone in mourning clothes, and bowed too to the men who carried the state's registers.
sentences.n: 式 shì is the crossbar at the front of a carriage, and so the verb 'to bow over the crossbar' (Zhu Xi: when there is someone to honour, one leans forward and rests on it). 凶服 is mourning dress. 負版 'carrying the boards': Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo both say these are men carrying the maps and registers of the state (邦國圖籍). Zhu Xi: he bowed to the two out of grief for those in mourning and regard for the count of the people; man is the most spiritual of all things and what the king takes as his Heaven, so in the Rites of Zhou the count of the people is presented to the king and he receives it with a bow — how much less could those below him fail to honour it? Kong Anguo takes 凶服 as the clothes and goods for sending off the dead (送死之衣物).

sentences.t:
有盛饌，
必變色而作。
sentences.l:
When there was a lavish meal,
he always changed countenance and rose.
sentences.i: Offered a lavish meal, he always rose to his feet, his expression altering.
sentences.n: 盛 shèng 'abundant, lavish'; 饌 zhuàn here is the meal served; 作 'to rise' (Kong Anguo: 起也). Zhu Xi: it was to honour the host's courtesy, not the food. He Yan's Kong Anguo: it honours the host's serving him in person (親饋).

sentences.t:
迅雷風烈，
必變。
sentences.l:
Sudden thunder, fierce wind —
his look always changed.
sentences.i: A crack of thunder or a fierce gale always made his face grow grave.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: 迅 is 'swift', 烈 'fierce'; his look changed in reverence for Heaven's anger. He cites the Record (the Book of Rites): if there is a fierce wind, swift thunder or heavy rain, one must change countenance, and even at night must rise, dress, put on one's cap and sit. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: reverence for Heaven's anger. Zhu Xi sums up 10.16: this section records the changes in Confucius's bearing.

sentences.t:
升車，
必正立，
執綏。
sentences.l:
Mounting the carriage,
he always stood square
and held the cord.
sentences.i: Getting up into his carriage, he always stood upright and took hold of the mounting cord.
sentences.n: 綏 suí is the cord one pulls on to climb into a carriage (Zhu Xi: 挽以上車之索也). Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: standing square and holding the cord, mind and body are all upright and sincere intent is grave and respectful; the gentleman's gravity is everywhere, and in mounting a carriage it shows in this. He Yan's Zhou Shenglie: standing square and holding the cord was for safety.

sentences.t:
車中，
不内顧，
不疾言，
不親指。
sentences.l:
In the carriage,
he did not look round behind,
did not speak hurriedly,
did not point himself.
sentences.i: Inside the carriage he did not turn to look behind him, did not talk fast, and did not point at things.
sentences.n: 内顧 'looking back' (Zhu Xi: 囘視也); 内 is the edition's form of 內. 疾 here is 'quick'; 親 'oneself, in person'. Zhu Xi cites the rites (禮曰): in looking about, one does not look past the wheel hub; all three lose one's bearing and unsettle others. His summary: this section records Confucius's bearing in his carriage. He Yan's Bao Xian: looking ahead no farther than the yoke-bar, to the side no farther than the side-rails and hub.

sentences.t:
色斯舉矣，
翔而後集。
sentences.l:
At a look, up it rose;
it circled, and only then came down.
sentences.i: One look at a man's face and the bird was gone; it flew round and round, and only when it had looked things over did it come down.
sentences.n: The subject, a bird, is not named; the next unit's pheasant may be it. 舉 is a bird's rising, 翔 its circling flight, 集 its alighting. Zhu Xi: it says that a bird, seeing an unfriendly look on a man's face, flies off, circles and looks carefully, and only then comes down to rest; a man, seeing the first signs, should act, and choose with care where he will stay, in the same way. But he adds that there must be text missing before and after this (此上下必有闕文矣). He Yan's Ma Rong: seeing an unfriendly look, it leaves; Zhou Shenglie: it circles and looks carefully, then comes down to rest.

sentences.t:
曰：「
山梁雌雉，
時哉！時哉！」
子路共之，
三嗅而作。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
He said: “The hen pheasant by the hill bridge —
how timely! How timely!”
Zilu set it out;
three times he smelt it, and rose.
sentences.i: The Master said: “The hen pheasant there by the footbridge on the hill — she has her season! She has her season!” Zilu served it up to him; he sniffed it three times and got up from his place.
sentences.n: The book ends on its hardest lines. Zhu Xi quotes Xing Bing: 梁 is a bridge; 時哉 says the pheasant drinks and pecks at the right time; Zilu did not understand, took it for a delicacy of the season and set it out (共具之, 共 read gòng); Confucius did not eat it, but smelt it three times and rose. Zhu Xi then gives two other readings: Chao Yuezhi (晁氏) says the Stone Classics write 戞 for 嗅, meaning that the pheasant cried out; Liu Mianzhi (劉聘君) says 嗅 should be 狊, 'to spread both wings' (citing the Erya). On those two readings, Zhu Xi says, 共 should have the sense 拱執 'to clasp the hands, hold' (his 又居勇反, gǒng) — so that, as we understand it, the three times would be the bird's, crying or spreading its wings before it rose. But he concludes that text must be missing here and no explanation should be forced; he records what he has heard to wait for one who knows. He Yan's commentary (unattributed) reads as Xing Bing does: the Master says the hen pheasant on the hill bridge has found its time while men have not found theirs, and so he sighs; Zilu, taking it for a thing of the season, served it up; it was not what the Master meant, and not eating carelessly, he smelt it three times and rose. 嗅 xiù 'to smell' (Zhu Xi: 許又反). Variant: He Yan's text writes 供 'to provide' for 共, which supports gòng. The book closes here.
